UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

Applicable AML statute: Law 10/2010 of 28 April on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, as amended; Royal Decree 304/2014 of 5 May approving its implementing regulation; Royal Decree 609/2023 of 11 July establishing the Central Registry of Beneficial Ownership (Registro Central de Titularidades Reales); Spanish Companies Act, Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 of 2 July; applicable EU AML legislation, EU financial-sanctions regulations, and Law 12/2003 of 21 May on the prevention and blocking of terrorist financing.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

A Spanish S.L. must have a registered office in Spain under Article 9 of the Spanish Companies Act. A virtual office may be acceptable for receiving correspondence and maintaining a registered address if the provider permits legal service and the address is genuine and registrable. It is not adequate as the sole operational substance for marine dredging, seawall construction, EPC contracting, port-authority work, equipment storage, environmental compliance, occupational safety, customs, or public procurement. The company should maintain demonstrable management, accounting, banking, contract administration, technical personnel, equipment access, and project records in appropriate locations. Sectoral permits, port concessions, environmental approvals, contractor classifications, and site-specific authorizations remain separate requirements.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central for name certification and the provincial Registro Mercantil of the registered office for inscription; electronic filing via CIRCE (Centro de Información y Red de Creación de Empresas).

Governing statute

Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010 (Ley de Sociedades de Capital), Articles 20 (subscription), 21 (minimum capital), 22 (paid-up capital), 25-34 (bylaws), 62-89 (SL administration and registration); Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (Real Decreto 1784/1996); Ley 18/2022 (Crea y Crece) for the Sociedad de Formación Sucesiva.

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura de Constitución de Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (Public Deed of Incorporation), inscribed in the provincial Registro Mercantil and published in the Boletin Oficial del Registro Mercantil (BORME).

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 41 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

Standard SL requires EUR 3,000 minimum capital fully subscribed and paid-up, evidenced by a bank scrow certificate from a Spanish credit institution; alternatively, the Sociedad de Formación Sucesiva regime (Art. 4.2 LSC as amended by Ley 18/2022) permits EUR 1 founding capital subject to mandatory retention of 20% of annual profits until capital reaches EUR 3,000.

Funding & unlock path: Fire safety certificate issued by the competent fire protection service in accordance with the Codigo Tecnico de la Edificacion and Real Decreto 513/2017 on fire protection installations; structural load inspection certificate (Inspeccion Tecnica de Edificios) for storage and plant areas; occupational health and safety clearance under Ley 31/1995 requiring an approved Plan de Prevencion de Riesgos Laborales before works start; port facility security clearance under the ISPS Code for all personnel and equipment entering restricted port zones.

Paid-in capital rule: Standard SL requires EUR 3,000 minimum capital fully subscribed and paid-up, evidenced by a bank scrow certificate from a Spanish credit institution; alternatively, the Sociedad de Formación Sucesiva regime (Art. 4.2 LSC as amended by Ley 18/2022) permits EUR 1 founding capital subject to mandatory retention of 20% of annual profits until capital reaches EUR 3,000.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT), including the AEAT Sede Electrónica for tax registration, tax identification number administration, VAT filings, customs procedures, and electronic tax communications. Certain regional authorities administer taxes devolved to Spain's autonomous communities, but national corporate income tax, VAT, and customs administration generally remains with the AEAT.

E-government filing portal

A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada must obtain a Spanish Número de Identificación Fiscal (NIF), generally consisting of the legal-person identifier letter and seven digits plus a control character. The incorporation workflow is: (1) obtain the company name certificate from the Central Commercial Registry; (2) execute the incorporation deed before a Spanish notary; (3) obtain a provisional NIF by filing AEAT Form 036 with the deed or incorporation documentation and the required identification of directors, shareholders, and tax representative where applicable; (4) register the company with the competent Commercial Registry; (5) file the registered deed or equivalent evidence with the AEAT to convert the provisional NIF into a definitive NIF; and (6) register the relevant business activities and VAT obligations through Form 036 before commencing taxable operations. A foreign shareholder or director generally requires a Spanish Número de Identidad de Extranjero (NIE) or, where applicable, a foreign-person NIF. A non-resident foreign entity conducting taxable activities in Spain must generally apply for a Spanish NIF through Form 036 and may need to appoint a Spanish tax representative where required by Spanish VAT rules, EU status, or the applicable tax treaty. The Spanish VAT identification number is the NIF prefixed by ES and is used for intra-EU transactions and VIES validation. Separate EORI registration is required for customs activity, including imports and exports.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada must obtain a Spanish Número de Identificación Fiscal (NIF), generally consisting of the legal-person identifier letter and seven digits plus a control character. The incorporation workflow is: (1) obtain the company name certificate from the Central Commercial Registry; (2) execute the incorporation deed before a Spanish notary; (3) obtain a provisional NIF by filing AEAT Form 036 with the deed or incorporation documentation and the required identification of directors, shareholders, and tax representative where applicable; (4) register the company with the competent Commercial Registry; (5) file the registered deed or equivalent evidence with the AEAT to convert the provisional NIF into a definitive NIF; and (6) register the relevant business activities and VAT obligations through Form 036 before commencing taxable operations. A foreign shareholder or director generally requires a Spanish Número de Identidad de Extranjero (NIE) or, where applicable, a foreign-person NIF. A non-resident foreign entity conducting taxable activities in Spain must generally apply for a Spanish NIF through Form 036 and may need to appoint a Spanish tax representative where required by Spanish VAT rules, EU status, or the applicable tax treaty. The Spanish VAT identification number is the NIF prefixed by ES and is used for intra-EU transactions and VIES validation. Separate EORI registration is required for customs activity, including imports and exports.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

A Spanish SL is ordinarily subject to Spanish corporate income tax as a separate legal entity and has no general United States-style check-the-box election to elect transparent or disregarded treatment. Limited statutory regimes and elections may apply, including tax consolidation for qualifying Spanish tax groups, the special regime for qualifying newly established companies, the Canary Islands Special Zone where eligibility requirements are satisfied, special regimes for qualifying holding companies or other regulated entities, and voluntary VAT regimes such as the monthly refund regime, the special cash-accounting regime, or VAT group treatment where statutory conditions are met. Spanish and EU anti-hybrid mismatch rules implement ATAD principles and can deny deductions, impose inclusion, or restrict relief for hybrid arrangements; they do not provide a general hybrid classification election for an SL.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general domestic turnover threshold applies for Spanish VAT registration. A person or entity must register before commencing, or when intending to commence, taxable business activities, acquisitions, imports, or supplies requiring a Spanish VAT identity. The small-business exemption threshold applicable in some EU jurisdictions does not operate as a general Spanish domestic VAT-registration threshold. A separate EUR 10,000 EU-wide threshold may apply to certain intra-EU consumer distance sales and specified electronically supplied, telecommunications, broadcasting, or electronic services, subject to the applicable OSS rules; it does not replace general Spanish registration obligations for a Spanish SL. Spanish construction, dredging, EPC, and infrastructure activities require transaction-by-transaction analysis of the place-of-supply rules, customer status, immovable-property connection, and any domestic reverse-charge rule.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

For goods, the Spanish VAT exemption with the right to deduct generally applies where goods are dispatched or transported from mainland Spain or the Balearic Islands to a destination outside the EU customs territory, and the supplier retains objective evidence of export and exit from the EU. The export declaration, transport evidence, commercial documents, and customs exit confirmation must be consistent with the invoice and transaction. Intra-EU supplies of goods may qualify for exemption with the right to deduct where the customer is VAT-identified in another EU Member State, the goods are transported to that Member State, and required reporting and evidence conditions are satisfied. Services supplied to a business established outside Spain may be outside the scope of Spanish VAT under the general B2B place-of-supply rule, rather than technically zero-rated. Services connected with immovable property, including many construction, breakwater, civil-engineering, and dredging works, are generally taxed where the immovable property is located; offshore performance, customer location, vessel status, and the precise contractual scope must therefore be analyzed. A maritime seawall or breakwater project located in Spain will generally not qualify as an export merely because the customer is foreign or payment is received from abroad. VAT refunds require valid purchase invoices, deductible business use, proper VAT books and filings, and evidence supporting any export or exempt transaction.

  • Electronic export declaration or Single Administrative Document equivalent, including the Movement Reference Number (MRN), commodity classification, customs procedure, exporter, consignee, value, and transport information
  • Customs decision or electronic confirmation of exit from the EU customs territory, such as the Export Accompanying Document or equivalent exit-results record
  • Commercial invoice, contract or purchase order, packing list where applicable, and transport documentation such as bill of lading, sea waybill, CMR, or air waybill
  • Evidence linking the exported goods to the Spanish supplier's VAT invoice and accounting records
  • Proof of delivery or destination evidence where necessary to establish the transport chain and resolve customs or VAT discrepancies
  • Import or destination-country customs evidence where available and relevant
  • Bank payment or inward-remittance evidence may support audit substantiation and anti-money-laundering controls but is not, by itself, a universal statutory condition for Spanish VAT export exemption and does not replace customs proof of exit

Spain does not currently operate a universal real-time VAT invoice-clearance system for all taxpayers. Immediate Supply of Information (Suministro Inmediato de Información, SII) requires qualifying taxpayers, including entities with annual turnover exceeding EUR 6 million, VAT groups, entities within the REDEME monthly refund regime, and voluntary participants, to transmit specified invoice-register data electronically to the AEAT generally within four calendar days, or eight calendar days where an invoice is issued by a third party or the recipient. Electronic invoicing is required in specified public-sector procurement through the FACe infrastructure and is subject to public-procurement invoice rules. The Law on the Creation and Growth of Companies provides for expansion of mandatory B2B electronic invoicing, but implementation depends on the enabling regulations and statutory transition periods; it should not be treated as a presently universal real-time clearance mandate without checking the applicable effective date. The VERI*FACTU invoicing-system requirements introduce standardized integrity, traceability, and anti-manipulation controls for qualifying invoicing systems, subject to the applicable implementation timetable. Spain has no general VAT digital-stamp requirement for ordinary invoices, although invoices must satisfy formal content, authenticity, integrity, legibility, and retention requirements.

Spain has no general statutory foreign-exchange repatriation deadline of 180 days for export proceeds. Export proceeds may generally remain abroad, subject to banking, anti-money-laundering, accounting, customs, transfer-pricing, and reporting obligations. If an export exemption or other VAT relief is unsupported, the AEAT may assess the unpaid VAT, statutory late-payment interest, and applicable penalties, together with correction of VAT deductions and related tax filings. Ordinary underpayment penalties may generally range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax depending on the seriousness, concealment, repeated conduct, or fraud indicators; the precise penalty depends on the breached provision and facts. False, manipulated, or inconsistent customs evidence can also trigger customs debt, import VAT, customs penalties, seizure or forfeiture measures, and administrative sanctions under EU and Spanish customs law. Deliberate fraudulent conduct may create criminal tax exposure where statutory thresholds and intent requirements are met. Voluntary correction before notification of an audit may reduce exposure under the Spanish General Tax Law, but documentary deficiencies cannot be cured solely by later bank remittance or retroactive invoicing.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain applies the EU Treaty principle of free movement of capital and payments. The euro is fully convertible on both current and capital account. There are no exchange permits for capital contributions, profit remittances, loan repayments, or trade settlements. Non-resident investors may freely repatriate dividends and liquidation proceeds, subject only to standard corporate income tax, withholding tax where applicable, and the submission of annual or statistical declarations to the Banco de España for amounts above EUR 50,000 or €100,000 thresholds. No dividend blockage or repatriation licensing exists. The sole practical hurdles concern banking compliance, anti-money-laundering documentation, and accurate classification of the payment purpose code.

Export proceeds surrender rules

There is no statutory obligation in Spain to surrender foreign-currency export proceeds or to convert them into euros. Export invoices may be issued in EUR or foreign currency; however, Spanish electronic invoicing and customs rules require accurate declaration of export receipts and, when payments are received in foreign currency, the underlying commercial documents must match the foreign exchange reference. For amounts exceeding statutory thresholds, exporters must report foreign-currency balances to the Banco de España for statistical balance-of-payments purposes. No mandatory conversion ratio or timing deadline exists because the euro is the domestic currency and the regime permits exporters to hold foreign currency accounts with Spanish banks, subject only to general reporting duties.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain), acting within the Eurosystem and in coordination with the European Central Bank; Spanish foreign exchange oversight is otherwise administered under EU Capital Movements Regulation and the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Medium feasibility with substantial legal constraints. A Spanish-registered fintech or electronic money institution (EMI) supervised by the Banco de España may provide IBAN accounts, payment initiation, and currency conversion services. Cross-border foreign fintechs operating under EU payment services passports can serve Spanish corporate clients on a branch or agent basis, but Spanish AML/KYC rules generally require the underlying corporate entity, its directors, and beneficial owners to complete enhanced due diligence before an operational account is opened. Pure offshore digital EMIs without a Spanish or EU-authorised passport are not viable for receiving capital escrow funds or supporting treasury flows because they cannot guarantee segregated client funds, Spanish tax identification (NIF), or reliable access to SWIFT and SEPA clearing. For an ISIC 4290 dredging EPC company, a bank-backed EMI may be used as a secondary collection rail, but the primary operating account should be held at a fully licensed Spanish credit institution to meet Port Authority milestone payment requirements and counterparty bank KYC expectations.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) is a non-resident corporate entity registered in a jurisdiction considered non-cooperative or blacklisted by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) or Spanish regulations.

Root cause: Ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) is a non-resident corporate entity registered in a jurisdiction considered non-cooperative or blacklisted by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) or Spanish regulations.

Defense evidence: Provide an independent corporate extract and certificate of good standing from the beneficial owner's commercial registry; detailed organisational chart tracing all intermediate entities; notarised and apostilled identification documents of all UBOs; audited financial statements for the last two years; declaration of source of wealth and source of funds; Spanish anti-money-laundering form of beneficial ownership (BOR); and a written explanation of the commercial rationale for the structure, accompanied by evidence of the direct link to the dredging project tender and the Port Authority contract.
Expected inbound capital contribution or initial escrow deposit has no clear purpose or references a sensitive origin-country jurisdiction.

Root cause: Expected inbound capital contribution or initial escrow deposit has no clear purpose or references a sensitive origin-country jurisdiction.

Defense evidence: Provide the executed shareholders' resolution for the capital contribution; notarised capital increase agreement; bank-issued certified draft or SWIFT MT103 with purpose code

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium feasibility with substantial legal constraints. A Spanish-registered fintech or electronic money institution (EMI) supervised by the Banco de España may provide IBAN accounts, payment initiation, and currency conversion services. Cross-border foreign fintechs operating under EU payment services passports can serve Spanish corporate clients on a branch or agent basis, but Spanish AML/KYC rules generally require the underlying corporate entity, its directors, and beneficial owners to complete enhanced due diligence before an operational account is opened. Pure offshore digital EMIs without a Spanish or EU-authorised passport are not viable for receiving capital escrow funds or supporting treasury flows because they cannot guarantee segregated client funds, Spanish tax identification (NIF), or reliable access to SWIFT and SEPA clearing. For an ISIC 4290 dredging EPC company, a bank-backed EMI may be used as a secondary collection rail, but the primary operating account should be held at a fully licensed Spanish credit institution to meet Port Authority milestone payment requirements and counterparty bank KYC expectations.

Statutory Filing Calendar

Annual Accounts (Cuentas Anuales) — balance sheet, profit and loss account, statement of changes in equity, statement of cash flows, notes to the accounts, auditor's report (when applicable) — approved by the shareholders' general meeting and deposited at the Mercantile Registry together with the annual beneficial-ownership confirmation (declaración anual de titularidad real). Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% on dividend distributions paid by a Spanish resident entity to non-resident shareholders, absent domestic exemption or treaty relief; domestic withholding rate applied by the payer when distributing profits; refund mechanism available where treaty rate is lower.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Within 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the fiscal year-end (e.g., for a December year-end, filing deadline is July 25 of the following year; if the deadline falls on a non-business day, it shifts to the next immediate business day); advance payments via Modelo 217 are quarterly (April 20, October 20, December 20) under the installment-payment mechanism.

Box-by-Box Return Breakdown (non-resident focus)

BoxField Non-resident guidanceTax-evasion pitfall
Box 1 (Identificación del contribuyente) Taxpayer identification number (NIF), corporate name, and tax domicile of the SL. Enter the Spanish NIF of the entity; non-resident shareholders are not reflected in this field; a non-resident owner with a Spanish permanent establishment must report the branch attribution separately. Late filing surcharge of 1% of the amount due per month of delay, up to 15% if filed spontaneously after the statutory deadline; if filed after AEAT notice, surcharge increases to 10% to 20% plus late-payment interest; failure to file without liquidation results in a minimum penalty of EUR 300 and maximum of 20% of the omitted amount; inaccuracies with criminal intent can elevate fines to 150% of the tax amount; late payment interest at the legal rate (currently approximately 3.75% annually, adjusted in the Spanish State Budget Act).
Box 2 (Período impositivo) Tax period start and end dates; must coincide with the civil exercise unless a corporate event triggers an abbreviated period. State the exact period of Spanish tax residence; a non-resident entity with a permanent establishment in Spain files for the full period of activity of that permanent establishment. Late filing surcharge of 1% of the amount due per month of delay, up to 15% if filed spontaneously after the statutory deadline; if filed after AEAT notice, surcharge increases to 10% to 20% plus late-payment interest; failure to file without liquidation results in a minimum penalty of EUR 300 and maximum of 20% of the omitted amount; inaccuracies with criminal intent can elevate fines to 150% of the tax amount; late payment interest at the legal rate (currently approximately 3.75% annually, adjusted in the Spanish State Budget Act).
Box 3 (Base imponible / Resultado contable) Accounting profit before tax adjusted for permanent differences, temporary differences including depreciation, provisions, and tax-exempt items. Compute the taxable base from Spanish-source income attributable to the permanent establishment; expenses incurred outside Spain are deductible only when properly linked to the permanent establishment's activity. Late filing surcharge of 1% of the amount due per month of delay, up to 15% if filed spontaneously after the statutory deadline; if filed after AEAT notice, surcharge increases to 10% to 20% plus late-payment interest; failure to file without liquidation results in a minimum penalty of EUR 300 and maximum of 20% of the omitted amount; inaccuracies with criminal intent can elevate fines to 150% of the tax amount; late payment interest at the legal rate (currently approximately 3.75% annually, adjusted in the Spanish State Budget Act).
Box 4 (Deducciones y bonificaciones) Domestic double taxation relief, international double taxation relief, tax credits for R&D, export activities, and reinvestment of nondistributed profits. Claim treaty relief by entering the corresponding credit under international double taxation; for non-resident shareholders receiving dividends, the credit is not claimed in this box because withholding applies at shareholder level. Late filing surcharge of 1% of the amount due per month of delay, up to 15% if filed spontaneously after the statutory deadline; if filed after AEAT notice, surcharge increases to 10% to 20% plus late-payment interest; failure to file without liquidation results in a minimum penalty of EUR 300 and maximum of 20% of the omitted amount; inaccuracies with criminal intent can elevate fines to 150% of the tax amount; late payment interest at the legal rate (currently approximately 3.75% annually, adjusted in the Spanish State Budget Act).
Box 5 (Cuota íntegra / Cuota líquida) Gross tax at 25% on taxable base, reduced after credits and prepayments to produce the final tax liability. Compute the final quota for the Spanish permanent establishment; no offset is allowed for taxes paid abroad on profits not attributable to Spanish PE activities except under treaty credit provisions. Late filing surcharge of 1% of the amount due per month of delay, up to 15% if filed spontaneously after the statutory deadline; if filed after AEAT notice, surcharge increases to 10% to 20% plus late-payment interest; failure to file without liquidation results in a minimum penalty of EUR 300 and maximum of 20% of the omitted amount; inaccuracies with criminal intent can elevate fines to 150% of the tax amount; late payment interest at the legal rate (currently approximately 3.75% annually, adjusted in the Spanish State Budget Act).
Box 6 (Retenciones y pagos a cuenta) Quarterly advance payments (Modelo 217) and withholdings from Spanish customers on invoicing applicable to construction and similar services; at least 1% retention applies to works projects, increased to 2% in certain cases. Reflect Spanish withholding certificates and AEAT payment receipts for the fiscal year; maritime dredging contracts with public authorities commonly trigger the special 2% retention on construction works if treated as construction contracts under Article 101 of the Personal Income Tax Regulation. Box 7 (Cuota diferencial) Final tax due or refundable after deducting all prepayments from the total liability. The differential quota may be reduced if the PE has paid excessive retentions; no additional tax relief arises from the shareholder's non-resident status. Mandatory designation of a Spanish resident individual or legal entity representative when the SL is controlled by non-resident directors and has no effective Spanish management; the representative must be vested with sufficient authority for filing and audit procedures. Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: EUR 1,000,000 of annual net revenues for entities required to prepare contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation (Local File) under article 18 of the Spanish Corporate Income Tax Law and Royal Decree 634/2015; Master File obligations apply when the group's consolidated revenue exceeds EUR 75 million; a simplified local file may be required when the entity is a constituent of a multinational group with Spanish operations and the related-party transaction value exceeds EUR 250,000, subject to the AEAT annual tax transparency form (Modelo 232) threshold of EUR 250,000 per related-party transaction type falling under the documentation regime.

Economic substance scope: Spanish law does not apply the UAE-style Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) as a distinct statute, but the substantive equivalent operates through the anti-abuse and substance-over-form doctrine: the general anti-abuse rule in Article 15 of the General Tax Law (LGT) permits recharacterisation of sham transactions; case law and AEAT practice require that an entity have premises, personnel, equipment, and effective management in Spain to be considered tax-resident and to avoid the lifting of limited liability; the corporate income tax residence test (Article 8 LIS) looks to incorporation under domestic law, registered office, or place of effective management; a dredging EPC company performing works through mobile maritime vessels must demonstrate Spanish establishment via vessel registry, local contracting office, and project management substance; failure of substance can trigger assessment on the actual beneficial owner, 150% penalty on the alleged improper deduction, and criminal referral under tax evasion rules.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax Evasion

Statutory sanction: Fine of 50% to 150% of the omitted tax amount under Article 191 LGT; for amounts exceeding EUR 120,000 per fiscal year, criminal tax fraud under Organic Law 10/1995 Article 305 carries imprisonment of 1 to 5 years; increasing to 2 to 6 years when fraud exceeds EUR 600,000 or uses shell entities that hamper collection; criminal penalty includes a fine of up to 6 times the defrauded amount.

Director personal liability: Directors jointly and severally liable for unpaid corporate tax under Article 43.2 LGT when responsible for the omission or for failure to wind up the company after dissolution; criminal liability extends to the de facto manager (gestor de hecho); travel bans, passport surrender, and preventive seizure of maritime vessels may be imposed; conviction carries disqualification from public funding and port concessions; civil restitution of the defrauded amount plus late-payment interest is ordered.
Transfer Pricing Misstatement

Statutory sanction: Assessment of a price adjustment to the arm's-length result plus late-payment interest; penalty of 25% on the hidden tax base for unassessed related-party transactions in the hands of the Spanish entity where documentation is absent or incomplete; incorrect documentation may attract a EUR 15,000 fixed penalty per omitted item up to a maximum of EUR 150,000, and non-submission of Modelo 232 incurs penalties of EUR 100 per data item with a minimum of EUR 1,200 and maximum of EUR 10,000.

Director personal liability: Directors who signed false transfer pricing documentation or knowingly signed non-arm's-length agreements are severally liable for the adjustment and penalty; audit exposure includes criminal referral for fraudulent falsehood where documentation is used to mislead tax authorities, with imprisonment from 1 to 5 years; the maritime dredging sector's heavy capital costs generate scrutiny of freight and hire charges, thus requiring vessel charter documentation, time-charter comparables, and crew cost analyses.
Shell Company and Lack of Economic Substance

Statutory sanction: AEAT and Spanish Land Registry courts may pierce the corporate veil under the doctrine of fraudulent incorporation; the company may be reclassified as a transparent entity, with tax assessed on the non-resident shareholder or actual beneficiary; administrative fine for abuse of legal form under Article 15 LGT up to 150% of the tax evaded; courts may order the monetary sanction of committing insolvency-motive dissolution and loss of the NIF for active operations; if the structure triggers anti-money-laundering examination for unexplained vessel ownership, penalties of EUR 1,500 to EUR 300,000 under the Spanish AML Law (10/2010) apply.

Director personal liability: Individual administrators, shadow directors and beneficial owners are jointly liable for the corporate tax of the SL when the company is unable to pay after being declared insolvent and the non-exercise of substance constitutes an aggravating circumstance; travel bans imposed by criminal courts if the vessel arbitration or port statutes are circumvented through shell companies; imprisonment up to 4 years for wrongdoing in the context of corporate insolvency under the Spanish Criminal Code; directors are disqualified from managing a Spanish company for up to 2 years in the event of abuse of the corporate entity.
Anti-Money Laundering and False Documentation

Statutory sanction: Copyright to the Spanish AML supervisor SEPBLAC: disciplinary fines of EUR 60,001 to EUR 5,000,000 for law-incident breaches under Law 10/2010; criminal laundering sanctions under Article 301-304 Criminal Code: imprisonment 6 months to 6 years plus fine of 1 to 6 times the laundered value; professional exclusion from public contracting for up to 2 years, cancellation of the dredging permit and exclusion from state procurement lists.

Director personal liability: Company directors whose vessel and cash flows replicate money-laundering typologies may face preventive arrest in satisfaction of bail for overseas flight risk, seizure of the sea-going vessels as instrumental goods in the crime, and civil compensation plus procedural costs; the maritime property registries are flagged for freezing orders, and directors may lose all limited liability exemption as LGT Article 42 imposes subsidiary responsibility for penal debts arising in the exercise of corporate management.
Late Filing and Unpaid Withholding

Statutory sanction: Article 192 LGT: fine of 50% to 150% of the unwithheld amount for the nonresident income tax; late filing of declarations without self-assessment: fixed penalty of EUR 200 plus a proportional penalty of 20% of the amount not paid; late filing of Modelo 200 after AEAT has served a prior notice results in a EUR 1,000 minimum penalty; interest from the date the amount should have been entered; criminal sanctions if unwithheld amount fraud exceeds EUR 120,000 in a single year.

Director personal liability: Directors who knowingly refrain from applying the Spanish withholding at 19% when declaring dividends to a non-resident shareholder are personally liable for the entire withheld quota plus penalty; if criminal liability arises, the company's administration body can be jointly sanctioned and the director may be prohibited from being a director of any Spanish company; Portuguese and EU arrest warrants serve as travel bans, and Spanish maritime firms risk forfeiture of the vessel as a means of payment for criminal fines.
